newsitem.title: FRANCE: Elections revive debate on French vision of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Elections revive debate on French vision of EMU.

text.p: France's political vision of European monetary union is likely to take centre stage in expected early elections -- with the main question being not whether EMU will happen but how and at what price.

At issue is whether Paris will back the hard-core, small currency zone favoured by Germany -- accepting that this will probably mean more austerity -- or seek a broader union, incorporating Italy, Spain and Portugal, one which might be less stringent on fiscal discipline.
Even before President Jacques Chirac's expected announcement later on Monday of snap parliamentary elections, political parties were staking out the ground.
Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin on Sunday ruled out a new bout of austerity to meet Maastricht treaty criteria.
"If, with the jobless rate we have..., we have to impose a new cure of austerity on the country to respect the (EMU) criterion of three percent, my answer is 'No'," Jospin said.
"'No' to the absolute respect of the three percent criterion," he said in a television interview.

That would tie in with his party's insistence that founder European Union member Italy, along with Spain and Portugal, should join EMU at the start -- likely, economists say, to require some fudging of a Maastricht treaty ceiling limiting budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
The ruling centre-right coalition, however, has already said it may need more spending cuts to meet the three percent target this year.
And if France is to go along with Germany's insistence that deficit reduction must be sustainable, the 1998 budget, to be presented in the autumn, is likely to be even harsher.
France infuriated the Bundesbank by allocating pension fund money held by state-owned France Telecom to the state budget to allow it to meet the three percent target this year.
If it is to soothe German nerves about a fiscally loose monetary union which might undermine the new currency, it may well try to avoid such "creative accounting" again.

And a tough French budget in the autumn would make it all the easier when it comes to deciding in early 1998 who qualifies for Economic and Monetary Union -- allowing Paris and Bonn to argue that their own budget cuts are sustainable, but that others, possibly including Italy's, are not.

Unlike the Socialists, the government has not stated its position on Italian membership of EMU, though a French government source denied on Friday that Chirac had told German Chancellor Helmut Kohl he had withdrawn support for Italy.

Economists said they were still puzzled by Chirac's apparent change of heart on early elections, which came shortly after a meeting in Bonn with Kohl where both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to launch the new euro currency in 1999.

But they said the need to push through a tough 1998 budget in the autumn appeared the most plausible reason, since the government seemed no more likely to win now than if it waited until the scheduled date in March 1998. "The basic reason for calling this election is so that they can tighten policy to get into monetary union," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
"It is entirely possible that Chirac took a bit of a scolding from Kohl," BIP economist Marie-Owens Thomsen said.

But even if it looked like the government was indeed seeking a new mandate for further austerity measures, economists said it would be difficult to campaign on the need for more public spending cuts at a time of record 12.8 percent unemployment.

People may start saying after years of belt-tightening that it was time to have a European policy to boost growth, said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard, who rated the government's chances of winning the election at 50-50.
Most people in the market believe the government will win.
It would also be difficult for the government to avoid taking a clearer position on what it thinks about early membership of EMU for Italy, Spain and Portugal.

"The question which arises is as follows: If the Germans say, 'We back the Maastricht criteria, we do not want Italy and Portugal', is the Left then obliged to destroy this concept of Europe, or not? That is the only question," French leftist Eurosceptic and former Socialist minister Max Gallo said.
